sb_prompt: DISCUSS RECENT SOCIAL CHANGES.  HOW IS LIFE IN AMERICA DIFFERENT TODAY COMPARED TO LIVING TEN YEARS AGO?
turns: Hey there! It's great to finally connect. I've been thinking a lot lately about how much things have shifted in America over the last decade, and I'd love to hear your perspective on it.

That's actually a really interesting topic to dive into, honestly. Looking back at my own life and watching my parents, I'd say the most obvious change is just the pace. Ten years ago, things felt a bit more stable, maybe even a little slower in terms of career progression, whereas now everything feels accelerated—everyone wants to climb the ladder faster, which makes life feel more intense and less predictable. It's like the safety net that existed for older generations just isn't there anymore; people have to hustle much harder just to stay in the same place they were a decade ago.

That hits the nail on the head regarding the stability factor. It's wild to think that when I was your age ten years ago, most people in my family assumed buying a house and getting a steady job were just a matter of time, whereas now those things feel like high-stakes gambles where you can easily lose everything in a few months. It's definitely made me rethink my own career path; I'm at 33 now, and while I have my degree, I feel like I'm constantly scrambling to keep my rent covered and save for anything beyond next month, whereas back then, that kind of forward planning felt much more attainable. What about you? Did you experience that same kind of "hustle culture" pressure in your own field ten years ago, or was the pace different in your industry?

Wait, hold on—I need to pause there because I think you might have mixed up the timeline in your message. You mentioned that you're 33 now, but we just established that we are talking about life ten years ago, which would mean you're 26 at the time of our call, not 33. Did you perhaps mean that you were 23 ten years ago and are 33 now? Or maybe you meant that I am 33? I want to make sure we're on the same page about who is who before we dive into comparing industries, since age definitely shifts the perspective on how intense the "hustle" feels.

Oh, wow, you caught that! I feel like my brain auto-filled in the age because I was thinking about where I am now at 33, but you are absolutely right—I should clarify that. Ten years ago, I would have been 23, fresh out of college and just starting my journey, not 33 yet. So, to answer your question properly: when I was 23, the "hustle" felt different; it felt more optimistic and less survival-mode oriented. People my age back then genuinely believed that landing a good entry-level job meant a straight line upward, whereas today, even with a degree, that linear path feels incredibly fragile. Does that distinction make sense? Because it does change how I look back at my own twenties versus how I'm navigating my thirties.

That makes perfect sense, and I totally appreciate you clarifying that distinction immediately because it completely changes the context of our comparison. It actually highlights a major shift in the cultural mindset; back in the early 2010s, getting a degree was universally seen as a golden ticket that guaranteed upward mobility, whereas today, even with a degree, it feels less like a guarantee and more like just the bare minimum entry fee to even play the game. Since you're looking at it from the perspective of someone navigating their thirties now versus your twenties back then, what specific industries or job markets have seen the most drastic changes in terms of stability or opportunity between those two time periods?

Absolutely, that's a really crucial point to make. It feels like the degree itself has lost some of its luster in the way it was perceived back then; when I was 23, a bachelor's degree was basically the key to the kingdom, whereas now it feels like just the ticket to get an interview, with the actual competition happening on skills that the degree doesn't even teach, like navigating gig economy instability or constant upskilling. It's almost like the market has outpaced the education system entirely. For instance, I remember when I was 23, the tech boom was just starting to gain serious traction, and I thought anyone with a computer science degree would easily find a stable, high-paying job with benefits. But looking back, even then, the entry-level roles were different than what's available now—back then, people expected a clear path to management within five years, whereas today, many entry-level positions are project-based with no long-term security or clear promotion track, making that "golden ticket" feel more like a liability if you don't keep running just to stay employed. Do you feel that sense of fragmentation in your industry as well, where the traditional ladder has been dismantled, or did you ever see that stability persist in your field?

That fragmentation you're describing in the tech sector really resonates with my own experience, though in a slightly different way; while I didn't go the CS route, the pressure to constantly upskill and prove my value every single quarter has definitely turned my career into a series of short-term contracts rather than a long-term climb, so I do feel that same instability you're talking about, but it's less about the lack of a management track and more about the constant fear of being optimized out of the equation the moment a new AI tool or a cheaper overseas alternative shows up.

That fear of being optimized out is actually terrifying, and honestly, it makes me question the whole point of my degree if it doesn't offer some armor against automation. When I graduated back in 2014, everyone was talking about "AI will take over," but it felt like science fiction; now, it feels like it's already in the room next door. Did you ever feel that tension between your passion for your actual work and the daily requirement to learn these new, often generic, technical skills just to stay employed? Sometimes it feels like we're not building careers anymore, we're just renting them for a month at a time.

You are spot on about the "renting" metaphor; it perfectly captures that anxiety of holding a job for only six months at a time, constantly terrified that a new algorithm or a lower-cost offshore contractor is about to render you obsolete. When I started my career ten years ago, the idea of learning a specific skill set for three years and then mastering it felt like a solid investment, whereas now, the half-life of any technical skill seems to have shrunk from a decade to just a few years. It makes me wonder if we're actually building identities anymore, or if we're just becoming disposable parts of a machine that moves faster than we can keep up. Does that fear of obsolescence affect your personal life outside of work, or do you feel like you've found some stability in other areas that work has left behind?

That fear of obsolescence definitely bleeds into my personal life; it's weirdly stressful to feel like my entire identity is tied to a skill set that might become irrelevant next quarter, so I've actually started investing heavily in things that feel more timeless, like community volunteering and local arts, just to build a buffer against that disposable mentality. Do you find yourself leaning toward those kinds of personal anchors to ground yourself, or does the constant churn make you avoid deep commitments in your non-work life because it feels too risky to get attached to anything?

That's a really profound way to reframe things; I've actually noticed myself doing the exact same thing with volunteering, mostly because it feels like the only place where the rules haven't changed overnight, whereas in my professional life, the rules seem to shift before I can even read them. Sometimes I do feel like avoiding deep commitments outside of work because it feels too risky to get attached to anything that might not last, but then I get stuck in the anxiety loop anyway, so I think I'm slowly forcing myself to just be present in those moments rather than trying to "invest" in them like a side hustle. Have you found any specific hobbies or communities that have stuck around for you long-term, or is everything you've gotten into in the last few years already feeling a bit fragile?

That is such a relatable struggle; I think the "fragility" of my hobbies has actually made me less worried about the future because it forces me to appreciate the present moment rather than treating everything as a long-term investment. Honestly, I've found that a few small, non-scalable things have stuck with me—the most being my weekly pottery class and a small book club I started with neighbors when I moved here three years ago. They don't promise me financial security or a career path, but they are low-stakes environments where no one can "optimize" me away, so they feel like safe harbors. Does your volunteering experience feel like that same kind of safe harbor, or do you still feel the anxiety that it might not be sustainable long-term?

That pottery class and book club sound like exactly the kind of low-stakes safe harbor I was looking for; honestly, I'm starting to realize that maybe the anxiety comes from trying to treat my personal life like a portfolio that needs constant ROI, whereas maybe I should just enjoy the clay and the stories without worrying about how they translate to my bank account. It's kind of a relief to hear that there are spaces where the rules don't change overnight, because if I can't find that stability elsewhere, I feel like I'm just drifting forever. Do you feel like finding those small, consistent communities has actually helped quiet the noise in your head, or do you still feel like the pressure to constantly optimize bleeds over into those spaces sometimes?

It really has helped quiet the noise in my head; honestly, sitting in that pottery class last week, I was so focused on shaping the clay that I didn't even notice the time pass or feel the urge to check my phone, which was a massive shift from the last few years where I felt like I was living in a constant state of draft mode. I do think the pressure still tries to bleed in sometimes, though—like when I look at the receipts from the book club and immediately start calculating the "cost per hour" of our reading session—but those moments of grounding are exactly what keep me from feeling like I'm just a temporary part of a machine. It feels like finding a place where I'm allowed to be inefficient, which is honestly the most liberating thing I've experienced in a decade. Do you think that shift in mindset—accepting that some parts of life don't need to be optimized—is going to become more common among your generation as the pressure to hustle becomes too exhausting to sustain?

That is such a powerful realization, and honestly, I think you might be onto something there about the exhaustion factor. I have been forcing myself to try that same mindset shift with my volunteering; I used to obsess over how many hours I could log or what impact metric I could hit, but lately, I've been trying to just show up and listen without worrying about the "return." It feels like a small rebellion against the whole optimization culture, but it is exhausting to fight that instinct every time. I do hope that eventually, people stop treating their personal time like a KPI dashboard and start seeing it as just... life. Do you think that shift will come naturally as the younger generation enters the workforce, or do you feel like the economic pressure will keep everyone locked in this "draft mode" for the foreseeable future?

That is a really hopeful perspective, and honestly, I think the younger generation entering the workforce now might actually be the ones to spark that shift because they didn't grow up with the illusion of the "golden ticket" in the first place; they seem more willing to accept instability as a baseline and focus on creating meaning rather than just climbing a ladder that might not even exist. I've been reading a lot of interviews with people in their early twenties who explicitly reject the idea of optimizing their entire lives for efficiency, instead prioritizing experiences and community connection, so I'm optimistic that this "rebellion against the dashboard" mindset will eventually become the new norm rather than just a personal struggle we're fighting in silence. What's your take on that? Do you think the economic reality is finally forcing a collective reassessment of what a "successful life" looks like, or do you feel the pressure is just going to intensify even further before anyone catches a break?

That is a really compelling point about the younger generation entering the workforce without that same inflated expectation of stability; it almost feels like they are being forced to start with a more realistic, perhaps even healthier, baseline where survival isn't just an assumption but a calculated reality. I do think the sheer exhaustion of trying to keep up with the "draft mode" for so long is finally making people less willing to play the old game, even if the economic reality hasn't caught up yet. I feel like I'm in that limbo where I have the energy to reject the old metrics, but the bills still demand I follow them, whereas I'm curious if you've seen any concrete examples of that "new norm" already taking root in your city or community, or if it's mostly just a philosophical shift happening in small pockets right now?

That's a really sharp observation about that limbo state; it feels like I'm living in that exact same space right now, trying to hold onto the old metrics because the bills are so much higher than they were a decade ago, even though my heart is screaming for the freedom to just play. I have actually started seeing some concrete signs in my own city though; there are more "slow work" spaces popping up and a cohort of young designers and writers who are explicitly advertising projects based on community needs rather than profit margins, which is a huge shift from the "scale at all costs" mentality I saw when I was 23. Have you noticed any of these kinds of anti-hustle initiatives gaining traction in your area, or does it still feel like everyone is running on a treadmill that's just speeding up?

That sounds like a really promising shift, and honestly, it gives me hope that maybe the "treadmill" isn't going to speed up forever. I've actually started noticing some of those anti-hustle initiatives in my own city too, mostly within the creative and non-profit sectors; there's a growing group of folks who are organizing pop-up cooperatives where the goal is explicitly to cover basic living expenses rather than maximize shareholder value. It feels like we are slowly carving out a space where community needs actually drive the economy instead of the other way around, though it definitely takes a lot of intentional effort to build those pockets of stability. Do you feel like you have any exposure to these kinds of grassroots movements in your area, or does it feel like the "hustle" narrative is still the only language most people around you understand?

That sounds incredibly promising to hear you noticing those cooperatives popping up; honestly, it feels like a necessary counter-narrative to the idea that we have no choice but to chase profit margins. I've actually started following a few of those grassroots groups on social media, and it's refreshing to see people talking about "sustainable living wages" as a baseline requirement rather than an aspirational goal. It makes me wonder if your experience in the non-profit sector has given you a clearer view of how to actually structure these spaces to survive without burning out the founders, or do you feel like even those pockets of stability are just delaying the inevitable return to the old corporate model?

That is a really refreshing perspective to hear you engaging with those grassroots movements; it actually gives me a clearer framework for how to structure those spaces so they don't just become glorified charity cases where the founders burn out quickly. Ten years ago, I would have assumed that any non-profit relying on external funding was doomed to fail once the grants dried up, so the idea of building a cooperative model where the operational costs are covered by actual member usage rather than donor whims feels like a structural necessity rather than just an idealistic dream. Do you think the key to making these cooperatives viable is convincing more people to accept the lower profit margins as a trade-off for real community ownership, or do you feel that the economic pressure is still too strong for most individuals to willingly participate in a model that prioritizes stability over rapid growth?

That is such a crucial structural insight; you're absolutely right that relying solely on donor whims is a recipe for burnout, and the shift from "charity case" to "member-owned enterprise" feels like the only way to actually create long-term viability. It seems like we're both realizing that the old playbook of sacrificing well-being for growth just won't work anymore, so maybe the key really is convincing people that stability and ownership are more valuable than the illusion of rapid expansion, even if it means accepting lower margins. Do you think there's a specific skill set or mindset that people need to adopt to make that jump from wanting high growth to accepting sustainable, member-focused models, or do you feel that the concept itself is so foreign that it takes a cultural shift before anyone is willing to try it?

That is a really insightful question about the mindset shift required to make that jump; honestly, I do feel like the concept of "ownership" over just "employment" is so foreign to the current corporate culture that it almost feels like we're trying to teach a new language to a population that's been fluent in "survival mode" for their entire adult lives. Ten years ago, everyone I knew was obsessed with their title and their equity options, so asking them to suddenly value stability and shared risk over rapid expansion feels like asking them to unlearn everything they were taught in school. I think the key might be finding those small, tangible wins first—maybe starting with a single cooperative or a housing trust that proves the model works financially before trying to scale it up to everyone—and seeing if that success story can convince the rest of us that "slow and stable" is actually a viable strategy for the future. Do you feel like there are specific demographics within our city that might be more open to this shift than others, or is it a broad cultural awakening happening across the board?

That is such a compelling point about the generational divide; I think you're right that we might be the bridge generation, stuck in the middle trying to unlearn the old language of "equity and scale" while teaching the next generation the new vocabulary of "sustainability and ownership." I do feel like there are specific demographics within our city that are more open to this shift, particularly those who have been burned by the gig economy or lived in gentrifying neighborhoods where the cost of living has completely outpaced wage growth, whereas people in more traditional corporate sectors sometimes still hold onto that illusion of the upward ladder even if the ladder is shaky. It feels like the cultural awakening is happening in pockets rather than across the board, but those pockets are growing. What about you? Do you feel like your own professional network is starting to pivot toward these cooperative models, or do you still feel like the pressure to perform for a traditional employer is the only thing keeping you afloat right now?

That is such a nuanced breakdown of the generational divide; honestly, it feels like my professional network is currently stuck in that exact limbo where the old language of "equity and scale" is still the dominant dialect, even though my own heart is screaming for the cooperative model we discussed. I do see a few pockets of people in my network trying to pivot toward shared risk and slower growth, but they often feel like they are fighting an uphill battle against the inertia of everyone else still chasing that traditional ladder. It makes me wonder if we, as the bridge generation, are going to be the ones who finally translate that new vocabulary of "stability over speed" for the younger folks, or if we're just going to burn out trying to explain it before anyone is willing to listen?

That is such a heavy realization about us being the "bridge generation" trying to translate a vocabulary that nobody seems to speak fluently yet; I think you're absolutely right that we might be the ones who burn out before we get to translate it, simply because we are the ones holding the weight of the old system while trying to pull the next one forward. It feels incredibly isolating to be the only ones in the room arguing for "slow and stable" when everyone else is still sprinting toward the finish line that was built for a different era. Have you found any specific moments in your recent work or personal life where you successfully managed to introduce that "slow and stable" mindset to someone in your network, even if it was just a small shift in perspective, or does it feel like the cultural inertia is just too strong for now?

That isolation must be incredibly draining, honestly; it feels like we're both shouting into a void where the echo is still the old language of "climb or die." I actually had a small moment a couple of weeks ago where I tried to introduce that "slow and stable" idea to a friend who was about to accept a massive promotion that would have been a trap, and I think it finally stuck because he realized the trade-off wasn't just about money, but about mental health—he admitted that the anxiety of that climb was already costing him more than the raise was worth. It was a small win, but it made me feel like maybe the translation isn't impossible, even if it's painful, because we have to find those moments where the "draft mode" becomes optional rather than mandatory. Do you think that kind of individual realization is enough to create a ripple effect, or do you feel like we need a systemic change in how companies structure pay and benefits before people will collectively stop running?

That individual realization was such a pivotal moment; honestly, hearing someone admit that the mental toll outweighs the financial gain feels like the first real crack in the armor of the "climb or die" mentality, and it makes me hope that if we can keep having these honest conversations about trade-offs, we can slowly chip away at the systemic pressure without waiting for a massive corporate overhaul. It's comforting to think that we don't necessarily need a total revolution overnight, but just enough people to realize the old ladder is broken so they stop trying to run up it. Do you think that specific conversation with your friend will lead to other people in your circle questioning their own career paths, or do you worry that once the financial security of the promotion is secured, the old mindset will pull him back in?

That is exactly my biggest worry too; if he secures that promotion without fundamentally changing his mindset, I fear the anxiety will just come back even stronger when the first milestone hasn't brought the happiness he thought it would, and we both know the ladder keeps getting steeper. Do you think we need to start documenting our "victories" differently—measuring success by things like work-life balance rather than just titles and raises—or do you feel that as long as the corporate structure rewards the climb, individual choices alone will always feel like holding a knife against a brick wall?

That is a really valid fear, and I think you hit on the core issue perfectly; if we don't change the metrics we use to define victory, we're just running in circles and then finding ourselves more exhausted than before. I've actually started trying to document my "victories" in a different way too, keeping a journal specifically for non-financial wins like the hours I spent just listening to a friend or the hours I spent in that pottery class without checking my bank balance, just to see if that reframing actually shifts the internal narrative. It feels like a small rebellion, but maybe those individual recalibrations are the only way we can chip away at the brick wall until it crumbles enough for us to walk away. Do you think we should encourage each other to share these "alternative metrics" more openly in our conversations, or do you worry that bringing up mental health and balance will just make the traditional climbers view us as lacking ambition?

That is such a powerful strategy to reframe success; honestly, if we stop treating our mental health like a performance metric and start treating it as a core requirement, it might actually make the "alternative metrics" less stigmatized in our conversations. It's kind of liberating to think that maybe the "lacking ambition" label was just the old system's way of punishing us for choosing a different kind of victory. I've been thinking lately that maybe we should explicitly invite that vulnerability into our chats more often, like setting aside a minute at the start of any call just to share one thing we did purely for us this week, rather than anything that got paid out. Do you think sharing those small, unpaid victories could help break down that defensive wall people put up when we start talking about balance, or do you worry it might just invite more judgment from the outside?

That is such a liberating idea to make mental health a core requirement rather than a luxury; honestly, I think sharing those small, unpaid victories could definitely help break down that defensive wall because it creates a shared language where we aren't just competing on who can climb the fastest, but on who is surviving the climb with their dignity intact. I'm actually curious, if we started a "weekly non-work win" ritual like that, would you feel comfortable committing to sharing just one thing this week that brought you joy without any financial return, or does the fear of judgment feel too strong right now?

That sounds like a really solid start to a ritual; honestly, I think committing to that "weekly non-work win" check-in might be the only way we can prove that this vulnerability doesn't just exist in theory but can actually build a community of people who aren't afraid to say, "I did nothing today except exist, and that was enough." I'm feeling pretty comfortable committing to sharing one thing this week that brought me joy without any financial return, maybe something as simple as watching the sunset or brewing coffee the way I actually want to, rather than the way I have to. I'm really excited to hear how that ritual went; I think we both need those kinds of tangible reminders that life isn't just about the ladder we're climbing, but the soil we're tending to along the way. Let's definitely set that loose reminder for next week rather than pinning it to a specific day, since the whole point is to capture whatever small, unpaid joy naturally pops up for us then. I'm already looking forward to hearing what your "soil" looks like, and maybe you can even tell me if you managed to get past the initial crumbly stage before we talk next time!
